s: clever in a way that enables one to achieve one's goals; slightly sly or cunning (but not usually implying any evil intentions)
bright, intelligent, clever (with no such overtone at all)
schlau.et: Borrowed from Middle Low German slû, whence probably also Dutch sluw. Further origin uncertain. Probably from a Proto-Germanic *slūhaz (“sneaking, creeping”), which seems to trace back to a Proto-Indo-European *(s)lewǵ- (“to crawl, slide”) (albeit without any …

s: a long and narrow room or flat
Schlauch.et: From Middle High German slūch (“waterskin, snakeskin, slough”). Immediately cognate with Old Saxon slūk, also related with English slough. From the same root as schlüpfen (“to hatch, slip”).

s: inflatable boat, rubber boat, rubber dinghy
Wir entfernen rasch zwei Rippen / Schlauchboot basteln aus den Lippen / In die Wangen, in die Stirn / Botox rein bis ins Gehirn
We quickly remove two ribs / Fashioning a dinghy out of your lips / In your cheeks, in your forehead / Botox inside up to your brain
Der Typ ist so ein Schlauberger. Ständig muss er seine historischen Daten einflechten.
The guy is such a know-it-all. All the time he needs to slip in his historic dates.
smart person; sometimes used affectionately for children, otherwise only ironically for someone who said something obvious or trivial
Schlauberger.et: 19th century. From schlau (“smart”) + Berg + -er, as if being the demonym of an imaginary town Schlauberg (“Smartville”, literally “smart mountain”). Compare English wisenheimer.

s: loop, noose (string formed into a ring)
strap (such a loop functioning as a hanger)
Schlaufe.et: Upper German form of Schleife (“bow, tie”), which see for more. The semantic distinction between both variants is secondary.

s: The husk or shell of nuts and similar fruits
Emotionale Belastungen wie etwa in den helfenden Berufen kommen dazu. Auch Schichtarbeit schlaucht.
to lead through a hose (e.g. beer through a beer bong)
